#1169. Steve Cherundolo names first U.S. U-23 roster on road to 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The road to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics is underway as Steve Cherundolo's roster for games against Scotland and Ukraine has been named, and it's an experienced group of players. Six players on this roster have been called up to the United States men's national team, and four earned caps during the recent September/October international break, while Parma's Benjamin Cremaschi was a member of the 2024 Olympic squad and is eligible to still be involved in the 2028 edition of the tournament.

Looking at the experience with eight players being based abroad and so many being on the fringes of the senior side, it shows just how deep the talent available to Cherundolo is for the Olympics during what is an exciting time for U.S. Soccer.

"We're very excited to bring this talented and polished group of players together and begin our journey toward the 2028 Olympic Games," Cherundolo said. "We're eager to get to work, establish our identity and build a strong foundation for what lies ahead. Our first international matches will be a great opportunity to challenge ourselves, compete, and grow together as a team."

They'll begin training for this camp alongside the senior team at the Arthur M. Blank National Training Center, similarly to how the United States women's national team set up their last camp. Not only does it showcase a synergy between the two sides, but it also provides both Cherundolo and Mauricio Pochettino with opportunities to oversee each squad, because when they're called next, considering how young the senior team is, too, there could be shifts between the two squads.

It's an important camp as it's Cherundolo's first since taking over the U-23s, so we'll get our first look at how the United States youth stacks up under him against solid opponents from around the world. Given the experience that's available to him and how tight competition will be for the Olympics, as three overage players can go in the 23-man squad for the competition, everyone will need to be on their game immediately.

#1168. Mauricio Pochettino breaks down in TEARS as he speaks out on 'most difficult decision' to leave US for Man United after agreeing to replace Michael Carrick at Old Trafford

Mauricio Pochettino broke down in tears as he began his farewell as US national team boss, and admitted that he couldn’t turn down the ‘dream’ job of Manchester United head coach.

United confirmed that Pochettino has agreed a two-and-a-half-year contract to replace Michael Carrick, and will start work on Wednesday after staying on for a double-header against Haiti.

Flanked by US Soccer Federation bosses at the team’s headquarters in Georgia, an emotional Pochettino wiped away tears as he thanked the players and staff.

‘I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,’ he said. ‘It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy.

‘When these moments arrive, it is always tough. Normally it is the opposite – you have been sacked! You cry because you want to stay.

‘I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward.

Mauricio Pochettino broke down in tears as he began his farewell as US national team boss

Pochettino spoke at a USMNT press conference after his move to Man United was confirmed

‘Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives.

‘In some part it’s a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.'

The 54-year-old Argentine revealed that United first made contact on Sunday after a 4-4 draw in Carrick’s final game left the club in the relegation zone.

United are paying US Soccer more than £10million in compensation to buy Pochettino and his backroom staff out of their contracts, and have allowed him to stay in charge for two more matches.

‘I never said I wanted to go back in the Premier League,’ said the former Tottenham, Chelsea and Southampton boss, whose first game in charge of United will be against Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday.

‘All of this was so quick because we arrived here last Friday and on Sunday afternoon this type of situation started to appear. There was some contact. When things became bigger, they are very sensitive.

‘We were very transparent with the federation and they understand the situation. The decision between US Soccer and Man United to agree to continue for these two games will not change our commitment.

‘That decision was between the three parties but, of course if Man United agreed different terms, I need to respect that.’

Pochettino, who will oversee his side's Concacaf Nations League quarter-final tie against Haiti over the next week, insisted it was the 'most difficult decision' to leave the USMNT

Meanwhile, Carrick issued a statement following his sacking on Thursday after 10 months in charge.

Posting on social media, he said: ‘I’ve had the immense privilege of leading Manchester United, the football club that I love.

‘There are very few who get to live that and feel it, and for that I’m incredibly grateful.

‘I want to say a big thank-you to the supporters. I must say, you are a special, rare breed.

‘I know we’ve not had the results lately, but you’ve shown me nothing but love and support in times when the easiest thing, and what most end up doing, would be to turn the other way.

‘That’s what makes you who you are. That’s why I fell in love with this club all those years ago.’

#1167. Wesley Fofana’s Chelsea nightmare continues as Liverpool win shoot-out

Unfortunately for Chelsea, Wesley Fofana put his hand up twice. Firstly to concede the first-half penalty for handball that allowed Liverpool to equalise quickly after Chelsea themselves had scored from the spot.

And secondly to volunteer to take one of the penalties in the shoot-out. The defender had to score to keep Chelsea in it, but he woefully, nervously skied his effort high into a gleeful Kop and it was Liverpool who went through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.

LIVERPOOL ARE THROUGH TO THE QUARTER-FINALS OF THE CARABAO CUP! 🔴 Wesley Fofana blazes over to hand Liverpool their FIFTH consecutive victory ✅ https://t.co/M4n01R8DSk

There the reward for Andoni Iraola, the head coach, is a home tie against the club he left in the summer: Bournemouth. The draw has opened up for Liverpool, and they know it, with only Manchester City left of the other big guns. But despite again playing at Anfield, they would have preferred not to face such a dangerous and motivated opponent, who have just reeled off five wins and five clean sheets in a row under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose.

This was also a big win. A meaningful win. One that was celebrated as such with Dua Lipa’s One Kiss – an anthem on Jürgen Klopp’s run to Liverpool’s first Champions League final under him in 2018 – played over the loudspeakers at the end as the players joyfully milled around the pitch.

One kiss is all it takes 🎶 https://t.co/0jfujy4V94

“I am happy to feel it. We feel the support,” Iraola said when asked whether he sensed the momentum and togetherness building in his reshaped Liverpool side. It looks as though they are.

Fofana was Chelsea’s eighth taker, so they were running out of options, but it was a truly terrible effort. The 25-year-old turned and scratched his head – just as many Chelsea fans have done over his underwhelming, albeit injury-hit, contributions since his eyebrow-raising £75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

Both sides had the chance to win it earlier in the shoot-out. For Liverpool it was Kostas Tsimikas, who had taken the decisive kick to beat Chelsea in a shoot-out in the 2022 FA Cup final, but the Greek full-back also completely missed the target.

Tsimikas has the chance to put Liverpool through... And fires over the bar! 😱 https://t.co/eCKBT6njMB

Then Chelsea striker Emmanuel Emegha – on his debut – saw his kick saved, after an effort by Ryan Gravenberch had also been stopped. In the end, Liverpool’s stand-in captain Joe Gomez – still to score an actual goal – crashed in his kick before Fofana’s blunder. The 29-year-old Gomez finally “scored” and it was an assured strike.

This was the fifth penalty shoot-out between these two clubs, in all competitions, with Liverpool having now triumphed in all five. They won the toss for this one and elected to take the kicks in front of the Kop, which roared its satisfaction and did its best to unsettle the Chelsea takers.

Both stand-in goalkeepers – Giorgi Mamardashvili and Mike Penders – made one outstanding save each in the shoot-out. Chelsea substitute Valentín Barco was the other player to miss, hitting a post.

Chelsea blink first in the shootout! 🔵 Valentín Barco's penalty bounces off the post... https://t.co/rSXGfQctbI

The other efforts, in truth, were outstanding and assured with Liverpool, undoubtedly, benefitting from Iraola turning to his bench and bringing on Alexander Isak, Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. All scored their penalties.

Among Chelsea’s scorers was Jordan Henderson and the former Liverpool captain received a strange homecoming in his first appearance at Anfield for three years. He was booed, in the first half at least, and especially when he tucked the ball under his arm before Chelsea took their penalty – in normal time – which gave them the lead. Henderson turned to the stands, grinning.

Morgan Rogers buries the spotkick! ⚽️ Chelsea take the lead at Anfield 🔵 https://t.co/YlDn2gakRi

In truth it was more pantomime than meaningful and Henderson, like another former, Champions League-winning Liverpool midfielder Xabi Alonso – now Chelsea’s head coach – did not celebrate as Morgan Rogers scored. The penalty came after a rash challenge by Gravenberch, who crashed into Moisés Caicedo as the Chelsea captain ran on to Malo Gusto’s shrewd reverse pass inside the area.

Afterwards, Alonso faced more questions about his decision not to use Estêvão Willian. Despite injury to João Pedro and Cole Palmer’s suspension, there was only a place on the Chelsea bench for the 19-year-old Brazilian. And he stayed there even though Alonso used all five substitutions. Estêvão has made just two starts under Alonso, both in this competition. “The season is long and there will be moments for everyone,” Alonso said.

It was hardly a ringing endorsement especially as Alonso brought on Emegha instead. The 23-year-old striker’s contributions amounted to having his shoot-out penalty saved and then bizarrely and violently charging at Virgil van Dijk – his fellow Dutchman, is there an issue there? – long after the ball had gone, pushing the Liverpool captain over.

Virgil van Dijk was NOT HAPPY with Emmanuel Emegha 😒 https://t.co/UEtoJ7n5va

Alonso said the exit was a “small set-back,” and maybe it was, even if he started with a stronger side than Iraola. But with Chelsea not in European competition and unlikely to win the Premier League, it means he is already down to the FA Cup should silverware be won this season.

There is no VAR at this stage of the competition but referee Darren England appeared to get all the big calls right. Rogers claimed a penalty before Chelsea’s one was awarded, but Ronald Araújo was probably just too strong.

Morgan Rogers wants a penalty but he won't be getting one 🙅‍♂️ The referee waves it away and there's no VAR to step in... https://t.co/VR6yhBrx0I

And Liverpool’s penalty? Just what was Fofana thinking? Only three minutes after the lead was gained, Chelsea relinquished it as Van Dijk rose to win a header and Fofana had his arm outstretched. The ball struck it and Cody Gakpo beat Penders from the spot.

SEVEN League Cup games at Anfield - EIGHT goals for the Dutchman 👏 Cody Gakpo is the Carabao Cup king 👑 https://t.co/KaysZedwYr

Little did we know then it would be the first of 17 penalties, 12 of them successful, in front of the Kop with the last being Fofana’s.

Fofana blazes into The Kop and Liverpool take their place in the League Cup quarter-finals. Liverpool have now won all five shootouts against Chelsea.

Liverpool beat Chelsea on penalties to reach the Carabao Cup quarter-finals! 🔴 https://t.co/pnCYwRrYzi

The Englishman has never scored a senior goal for Liverpool but emphatically smashes this into the top right corner.

Mamardashvili guesses correctly and makes the save to his right.

Penders makes the save and Chelsea, who now have the chance to go through.

The Englishman lifts it high into the net and we go on.

An emphatic penalty from the Frenchman right into the top left corner.

The former Liverpool captain has to score and he does, sending it down the middle. To sudden death we go...

The Greek defender has a chance to seal Liverpool’s place in the final eight but sends it over the bar.

The Argentine strikes the left post and Liverpool will have the chance to book their place in the quarter-finals with their next penalty.

The German makes no mistake, sending Penders the wrong way and putting it into the bottom right corner.

The Belgian calmly steps up and sends Mamardashvili the wrong way, putting into the right corner of the net.

The Dutchman scored Liverpool’s equaliser from the spot and smashes this one into the bottom left corner, with Penders going the wrong way.

He scored during the game and finds the net again. Mamardashvili goes the right way but the penalty from Rogers is very good, going right into the bottom left corner.

Again, Penders guesses the right way but, like Mac Allister, Isak lifts it brilliantly into the top of the net.

The Portuguese finds the net and we are all square after one penalty each.

Penders went the right way but Mac Allister lifts it over the Chelsea keeper.

They will be taken at The Kop. Chelsea goalkeeper Penders disappeared down the tunnel after the full-time whistle and re-emerges with a towel, potentially some penalty-saving notes as well?

Liverpool will take first and it will be Mac Allister who steps up first...

The final whistle is blown so we go to penalties at Anfield.

Looks like we are heading for penalties and if you are looking for omens... Liverpool and Chelsea have had four shootouts in the past: Liverpool won them all - the 2007 Champions League semi-final, the 2019 European Super Cup final, the 2022 League Cup final and the 2022 FA Cup Final.

A word on VAR (again). Watching this competition without the presence of the joy-killing invention is liberating. An occassional decision might get missed but, in the long term, you could live with that if meant you didn’t hear the words “it’s being checked by Stockley Park”. The decision just before, when Florian Wirtz’s shot touched Levi Colwill’s hand, was a case in point. It wasn’t a penalty but VAR being brought into play might convince you it was. Let’s get rid of it, please.

Double change for Liverpool as Isak and Mac Allister replace Ngumoha and Nyoni.

Huge double block from Chelsea and how have Liverpool not scored? Tsimikas’ cross to the back post is headed back across the six-yard box to find Wirtz, who you think is going to score but Colwill makes the block. Then Barcola has a shot blocked by Acheampong.

It is full time at both Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light, where Crystal Palace and Sunderland have booked their places in the League Cup quarter-finals.

Tsimikas gives it away inside his own half and Chelsea counter. Neto drives inside and finds Rogers, who skips past Gomez. Rogers then finds the overlapping Palestra on the left side of the box and the Italian is denied by Mamardashvili at his near post.

Manchester City have just beaten Brighton 4-3 on penalties whilst on the south coast Bournemouth have comfortably beaten Aston Villa 3-0. Both sides are into the hat for tonight’s quarter-final draw.

Lavia cynically brings down Ngumoha as the Liverpool forward drove through the Chelsea half and is correctly booked.

Liverpool are taking off Van Dijk and Jacquet is coming on in his place. No injury for Van Dijk.

What a terrific cup tie this has been. It helps when there is an edge between the sides and you can feel the tension in the air. What has been noticeable in the last three games at Anfield, though, is the change in the atmosphere. Slowly but surely the locals are buying into what Andoni Iraola is trying to achieve. Liverpool could lose this game tonight by going all out to win it but there is a clearly identity developing that makes you think they are starting to get on the right lines.

After Gakpo fouls Lavia, Chelsea have a free-kick just over 25 yards out. Rogers lines it up but his effort is terrible, flying into The Kop.

Chelsea are going to make a triple change. Palestra, Barco and Emegha come on, with the latter on for his Chelsea debut. Gusto, Caicedo and Welbeck head off.

Good save from Penders. The ball comes to Barcola outside the Chelsea penalty area. The Frenchman drives inside before getting his shot away from the edge of the box. The shot takes a small deflection and Penders does well to make the save down to his left.

The game between Manchester City and Brighton at The Etihad has ended 2-2, therefore it has now gone to penalties.

Chances at both ends. Gomez whips in a cross from the right and picks out Araujo in the centre of the box but the Uruguayan’s powerful header is straight at Penders. He probably should have scored.

Then Chelsea counter and Rogers is in acres of space. His shot from just outside the box takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner, which comes to nothing.

Gusto’s behaviour in recent minutes has been appalling. First he went down after virtually no contact from Van Dijk and now goes down again, once more not a foul. He shows his boot to the linesman as if it came off in a challenge from Barcola but the replays show that his boot did not come off and he was attempting to con the officials.

Andoni Iraola is turning to his bench for the first time tonight and makes a double substitution as Wirtz and Barcola replace McConnell and Koumas. Some double change that for Liverpool!

Fascinating to watchg Trey Nyoni and the responsibility he has taken on his shoulders. He’s only 19 but those who have worked with him since he arrived at Liverpool as a 16-year-old will tell you he has a maturity of someone in their mid-twenties. He has tried to get on the ball and play, he’s been strong when it’s been required and always been in the right place to get a foot in. He’s going to play a lot of games for Liverpool if he maintains this trajectory.

Achemapong scythes Ngumoha down as the latter cut inside and the former is correctly booked.

#1162. Chasing dynasty: How Gotham FC's NWSL Shield win completes transformation ahead of playoffs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

En route to their second NWSL championship in two years, relatively new Gotham FC recruit Jaedyn Shaw was uninterested in the narratives that underestimated her team. The surprise win at the NWSL Shield-winning Kansas City Current in the playoff quarterfinals was not a surprise to her, and she made it clear with three quick words: "Underdog, my ass."

Shaw had a point on that cold day in the Midwest, and almost exactly a year later, it still stands. Gotham are the NWSL's new dynasty, and their Shield win marked their fifth major title in three years, with a sixth in their sights as the playoffs begin this weekend. The transformation was rapid for a team that has historically been a bottom-dweller, so much so that their 2023 championship triumph was a genuine surprise. They quickly built a title-winning team and reaped the rewards just as swiftly, but even as the muscle memory of title charges returns, Gotham will go about their next NWSL playoff journey differently. The target is officially on their backs, the onus officially on them to live up to the billing.

Gotham have played the vast majority of their playoff games as the lowest-seeded team in the postseason, winning the championship twice in those circumstances. Sunday's quarterfinal against the Seattle Reign, though, will be the first game they play as the unquestionable favorites to win the whole thing. How Gotham will play with the weight of expectations is entirely unclear, since they have never done it before, but it is a good problem of their own creation, one they have chased since the 2023 triumph.

Date: Sunday, Nov. 8 | Time: 12:30 p.m. ETLocation: Sports Illustrated Stadium -- Harrison, N.J.TV: ABC | Live stream: ESPN AppOdds: Gotham FC -150; Draw +265; Seattle Reign +340

Their blitz in the free-agent market in the winter of 2024 laid the foundation for their dynastic run, but the most fascinating feature of Gotham's years-long run of success is the evolution they have undergone since. U.S. women's national team defender Tierna Davidson has become the team's captain, her progressive passing ability making her a key fixture in head coach Juan Carlos Amoros' system. Her club and country teammate Rose Lavelle has become a standout, but the star of the show has been Shaw, who has barely missed a beat since her arrival in September 2025.

Shaw has 14 goals and seven assists in 35 NWSL games with Gotham, her wide-ranging skill set fully on display in Amoros' team. She has been a little bit of everything for the team's attack, which is arguably too reliant on her talents, but it is almost hard to fault Amoros for the approach. The system has allowed Shaw to flourish, in particular bringing out a clear goal-scoring quality that is key to a Gotham team that values defensive work rate first.

"First, I think the commitment they have to defend and the commitment they have to work hard for the team despite being some of the best players technically in the planet," Amoros said about both Shaw and Lavelle after a win over the Chicago Stars in September. "I think that helps the connection, not only between them two. There is a mutual respect there because of that but then also from the whole team. When you have to play and those are the players that produce the chances for us in the final third but then the people that [are] behind them are always supportive of them because of the work they put in and then we try to work a lot with them to how we can find them and how they can connect more with each other and the same with Sam [Kerr]."

He has found a unique way to make Shaw and Lavelle work together, despite the fact that they appear to have overlapping skill sets when it comes time for USWNT head coach Emma Hayes to slot them into her lineup. The pair often play just behind Kerr, an out-and-out striker, and assume the role of strikers themselves while balancing their creative tendencies. They have filled in some gaps along the way -- Kerr, for example, ranks third in the league with 9.67 expected goals since returning to the NWSL on July 16 but has scored just four times. Kerr does, though, have four assists in 17 games, one fewer than Shaw and one more than Lavelle over that span.

The connection between Lavelle and Shaw has offered Gotham a level of dynamism that has been missing in their attack at times over the years, even as they racked up title after title. It helps that the two have enjoyed working alongside each other, the 21-year-old Shaw in particular taking inspiration from Lavelle, a decade her senior.

"I think her movement is some of the best in the world, honestly," Shaw said after that September win over the Stars. "She's able to make stretch runs, drag players. She attracts so many players, opening up space for other players to get on the ball and then getting on the second one, I think, is one of her strengths and is something I'm trying to replicate off of her. I think she's just incredibly smart in soccer knowledge."

For each of them, a return to fitness after small injuries in the final weeks of the regular season comes not a moment too soon. Kerr's inconsistency is not the only attacking issue they will need to overcome -- Jordyn Dudley will miss the postseason with a foot fracture she sustained last month, her impressive rookie season coming to a close with four goals and three assists. Lavelle and Shaw will be particularly useful against the Reign, whose defensive qualities continue to be a strength.

Shaw has become the focal point of Gotham's reinvention in recent years, but Amoros' side has added experienced options in a wide variety of positions since the 2023 championship. The vast majority of Gotham's likely starters on Sunday will have joined the club after the 2023 playoff run, a steady stream of important players signing themselves up since. Ann-Katrin Berger, the 2024 goalkeeper of the year, made the move not long after Davidson and Lavelle did, and European champion Jess Carter followed right after. Midfielder Jaelin Howell, who has been in and around the USWNT, was recruited in time for the 2025 season, and Shaw joined months later. Left back Guro Reiten has two goals and six assists since making her club debut in April, while Kerr made the move at roughly the same time as midfielder Denise O'Sullivan, a two-time NWSL champion with the North Carolina Courage.

Gotham's reinvention is constant, the core evolving each and every season. It is a unique route to the top, but in another season of change, they found the consistency they have been chasing since the 2023 championship. The underdog label has well and truly been shed, the team chasing another tag entirely -- a third championship would put them level with the Portland Thorns as the most successful team in the league's history.

#1160. Kai Havertz leads the Premier League in offsides as Arsenal pile up infractions in 1-0 win over Hull City

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LONDON -- Though there was some to-ing and fro-ing as to the order in which the offenses should be considered, it seemed fitting that what would have been Arsenal's best scoring chance of the first half of their 1-0 win over Hull City was wiped out for an offside. Here is a team whose attack has been drifting so out of sync that promising situations fall apart without the opponent needing to get involved.

Sometimes the opponent is even willing to offer them a helping hand. Only the members of the International Football Association Board might be able to say for sure whether Arsenal should have had a penalty when Kai Havertz's shirt was pulled by Hull City's Nobel Mendy as Bruno Guimaraes took a long-range shot. The striker was impeded, but he had been standing in an offside area. Was he attempting to play the ball when Mendy grabbed hold of his jersey? If not, then the foul should have taken precedence and Arsenal should have had a penalty. Instead, they had to wait until the 72nd minute for their win, Martin Odegaard bundling in the rebound off Noni Madueke's shot.

At least that meant Mikel Arteta could jokingly say he had not seen the spot kick that might have been. There may be a question about that particular penalty and offside, but the big-picture statistics are mind-boggling, such that there surely has to be some air in these numbers.

In the last seven Premier League seasons, no team has averaged more than three offsides per game. Only Burnley in 2021-22 and Liverpool two years later have averaged more than 2.5, in the process reaching over 100 for the season. In their 10th game of the season, Arsenal committed offside offenses Nos. 32, 33, 34 and 35. At the final whistle, that was 11 more than any other team in the league, and there is a very real prospect that lead does not get eaten into. Field a team of Pippo Inzaghis and you'd do well to put up these numbers.

There has to be something to this, right?

What makes this all the more curious is that Arsenal have not been a team that particularly struggled to stay onside before this season. In the previous six campaigns, they were caught about as often as the average Premier League team when you adjust for possession. When these relatively low-volume statistics warp like this, at least part of the answer is going to be variance. A bit more of it might be that Arsenal have a 10-game sample size that includes Aston Villa. Still, that sample is over a quarter of the season. Arsenal have had a string of games where they have been caught offside with frequency.

This looks like a problem. Even Arteta acknowledged that. "There are many areas that we need to improve. That's one, that's related sometimes to the timing or the situation, or really the position [of the opponent], where he's lined up and what space he's given you.

"Certainly it's far too many. It's true that the Villa game obviously he's putting those stats in a different perspective. I think the sample is quite short to analyse it, but you have a point there."

As for the Villa game, Mikel, yes, that's eight of your 35. Leeds is seven, though. Coventry five, Hull four. These are all well above the Premier League average. The chief culprit for this spate of infractions is certainly Havertz. His 15 offsides are not just seven more than any other player in the top flight; they are more than any Arsenal player committed in the entirety of last season's title campaign.

Again, this feels a little unprecedented. In the six seasons prior to this one, Havertz ranked 48th among forwards in the division for how frequently they were caught offside. The worst offenders, your Ashley Barneses, Darwin Nunezes and Cristiano Ronaldos, might get flagged once every 70 or 80 minutes. Havertz hovered around the 140 mark. This season it's not far off once per half.

Has he lost some burst? Gradient Sports' physical data would suggest he is moving about as swiftly this season as any other. A broader view is that this attack might have greater joy punishing high lines with more pacey options in it. For a player who makes so many runs off the ball, Madueke is caught offside relatively infrequently (though his was one of the four today). That is probably because he can give his man a yard in a way that Havertz or even Bukayo Saka, third in the league with seven offsides, can't quite.

Have defenses sussed Havertz's movement out? That doesn't seem entirely clear, not least given that Hull misjudged their line more than once, allowing Havertz in a one-on-one position where he should have done much better than cut the ball onto Mendy's trailing leg.

Arteta's explanation is simple. "It's all about timing," he said. "So there is a signal on the ball, and you need to time it around that. If that's a second too late or half a second too late, that's all."

Certainly Arsenal could release the ball a bit quicker. If there is a flaw in the game of Odegaard, whose nine passes to an offside teammate also lead the league, it is that he tends to want that one extra touch. That much was apparent in the win at Aston Villa, when the captain had the ideal chance to slip Havertz through in position to bend one in the far post. He took three touches when two would have sufficed, and it was all a moment too late.

Bruno Guimaraes (four such passes) is in a similar vein. And perhaps Arsenal as a club are a bit too much of that ilk. Does the specter of Alex Hleb and Samir Nasri still haunt this team? Arteta might have said as much, that the thing about Arsenal is they always try to walk it in.

"We need to find ways to be more efficient, sometimes even more pragmatic," he said. "Sometimes my feeling is that we are trying to score a perfect goal against these low blocks. We need to be much more chaotic than that."

You can see that in some of those offsides above, especially the smattering around the right flank that Arsenal like to make their creative hub. It's the attempted reverse balls, the quick one-twos and slide-rule passes to a teammate on the overlap. Offside No. 36 might well have been another of those, an overlapping run from Jurrien Timber where Madueke released the pass a beat too late and the Dutchman stopped rather than cede Hull a free kick.

Instead, Madueke proved the value of an alternative approach right throughout this match. Driving at his fullback time and time again, he manufactured positions where things might happen without having to worry about a give-and-go or timing his run correctly. In an age where so many opponents, including Hull, are more intent on gumming up their opposition than gritting and grinding, a bit of unpredictability from one of Arsenal's own players goes a long way. As for the offsides, of course that feels like a problem, a lot of possessions wasted by Arsenal players' own inability to get on the right beat. It has been. It does not mean it is going to be. Injuries mean that Havertz and Odegaard have rarely shared the pitch over the last few seasons. Get them and Saka together for weeks on end and the old rhythm will come back to them, and this should be nothing more than a weird, if intriguing, blip.

#1158. Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Climate change is affecting many types of crop, including these unusually small potatoes.Credit: John Thys/AFP/Getty

Policymakers at the United Nations COP31 climate conference that started this week in Antalya, Turkey, will know that the UN Environment Programme has confirmed that global warming will exceed the limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures agreed in 2015 in Paris. This meeting comes hot on the heels of the UN COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, which affirmed yet again that the world is also in the middle of a biodiversity crisis. Progress in each case, whether preventing dangerous climate change or stemming biodiversity loss, is too slow. But researchers across scientific disciplines are now arguing that advances in biotechnology could provide solutions1. Methods such as gene editing and germplasm mining — the analysis of huge libraries of plant-genome sequences to find useful traits for crop improvement — can now be used to tackle global warming and protect nature, scientists write in a climate-themed issue of Nature Biotechnology.

There was a time — not that long ago — when many considered biotechnologies a threat to the environment. But as the special issue shows, a shift is under way. Now, the field offers strategies for protecting both climate and biodiversity from the many damaging effects of industrial agriculture.

To feed a growing global population, between 2015 and 2024, the amount of cultivated land grew by roughly eight million hectares a year1. Yet, if the greenhouse-gas emissions, and thus global warming, this expansion causes is to be avoided, the world must work out how to produce enough food within its current agricultural footprint. Land clearance and land-use change contributes up to five billion tonnes of carbon annually — and is a major cause of biodiversity loss. Here, biotech solutions have some of the greatest potential, for example, by helping to increase crop yields and to protect plants from heat, drought and disease.

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

Of 77 such technologies with applications in agriculture, aquaculture and other sectors, many are ready for large-scale testing in the field, propose bioengineers Shekhar Mishra, Lauren Lui and Adam Arkin at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California in a Perspective article2. Argentina, China and the United States have given the green light to engineered drought-tolerant crops.

Rice farming produces around 9% of human-caused emissions of the greenhouse gas methane. Now, researchers have found a way to slash these emissions, write agronomist Yunkai Jin at Hunan Agricultural University in Changsha, China, and his colleagues in a Comment article3.

But technological readiness isn’t enough: governments, regulators and the public need to be ready, too4. Readers might have a sense of déjà vu: in the 1990s, advances in biotechnology promised a revolution in food and agriculture — which subsequently stalled. The ambition was to genetically modify crops or engineer them in other ways so that they could tolerate herbicides, resist insects and fight viruses. But, at the time, many scientists, governments and corporations promoting the technology gave insufficient attention to several issues.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

One concern was public anxiety about the idea of eating food produced using transgenic technologies — crops modified by inserting a gene from another plant species or other organism. Another issue was that risks to the environment and to human health had not been studied sufficiently. A third problem was that multinational companies dominated both the research and the development of these technologies, creating fears that the rise of agricultural biotechnology would put many small family farms out of business.

Environmental groups found common cause with consumer organizations. Together, they urged governments to enact strict regulations. In the European Union, for example, risks to human health and the environment needed to be assessed before technologies producing genetically modified organisms could be commercialized. Although this was necessary, it slowed down advances in low- and middle-income countries, because any nation intending to export produce to the EU would have to prove that it was not genetically modified.

Since then, at least two things have changed, increasing optimism about the use of biotechnology to help the planet. The discovery of gene editing — in which an organism’s genes are modified precisely to produce specific traits — has proved transformational for agriculture. The method is being developed cautiously and is regulated in a more nuanced way than were conventional technologies that produce genetically modified crops. In June, the EU amended its regulations on genetic modification and now permits the cultivation of some gene-edited crops.

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

A second development is that catastrophic events such as heatwaves and floods have meant that climate change and the planet’s protection have become mainstream concerns across science and society, not just for environmental research. In a way, we all need to be environmentalists now, and this provides a rationale for governments to reconsider adopting biotech solutions with appropriate safeguards in place.

Advances in biotechnology that limit land use should be deployed to slow down the rise in global temperatures and biodiversity loss. This will require a partnership between the private sector, scientists, conservationists and farmers. High-yielding crops produced using industrial agriculture have helped to feed the world but have also had a devastating effect on biodiversity. Organic agriculture is more sustainable but requires extra land, because its yields tend to be lower than those from industrial methods. Providing they are implemented wisely, safely and ethically, biotechnologies could contribute to innovative farming methods that offer the best of both worlds.

#1155. Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N

The last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

The whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

HARRISON, N.J. – Gotham FC head coach Juan Carlos Amoros criticized the field conditions at Sports Illustrated Stadium during the team's 1-0 win over the Seattle Reign on Sunday, a complaint that highlighted the infrastructure battles the league is grappling with during this season's playoffs.

The NWSL fined Gotham $10,000 in the build-up to Sunday's quarterfinal over the quality of the pitch, which appears to have been overworked in recent weeks. Gotham are a secondary tenant at the stadium, which is owned by New Jersey's Hudson County and is primarily the home of the Red Bull New York. The MLS team played their regular season finale on Saturday evening, less than 24 hours before the 12:30 p.m. local time kickoff for the NWSL match. The stadium also hosted a rugby doubleheader the previous week, the scars of which were easy to spot over the course of Sunday's game.

"I feel the obligation to almost apologize for the state of the pitch," Amoros said post-match. "I think at this level, in this kind of game, as a league, we should be having a better surface. Unfortunately, our football club did absolutely everything in their power to make sure that was the case. Unfortunately, it wasn't but luckily, it looks like nobody got hurt and the game was what it was."

Players on both teams complained of the playing conditions, including Gotham's Jaelin Howell, who worked her way back from an ankle issue in time for Sunday's match.

"Obviously it's pretty sandy out there and so a little unstable but I want to be able to give my all to the team and everything I got and so obviously can't think about that," Howell said. "The other team has to play on that, too, so we acknowledged it and we moved on and I think that our team managed it pretty well for the most part."

The Reign's Jess Fishlock, a member of Seattle's squad since the inaugural NWSL season in 2013 who played the final match of her career, was more harsh in her assessment of the field.

"We performed so well for this group of players to come against a team like that at home on this field, which is atrocious, just saying it out loud," she said.

Her comments were echoed by Reign coach Laura Harvey, who has worked in and around the league since its inception.

"Let's be real, there's no way a playoff game should be played on that shit," she told ESPN post-match. "I just can't believe they've allowed it. They knew it last week."

Amoros said the field conditions ultimately impacted Gotham's ability to perform on Sunday, the NWSL Shield winners stringing together a performance he described as "not the best football match that you will ever see."

"When you play on a pitch like that, you cannot be thinking of the next action or what you're gonna do once you get that ball," he said. "You need to be looking at the ball because he can bounce at any given time. Plus, it just changes the whole dynamic of the game and it changes the dynamic of how we play. We adapted certain things. We adapted certain things on the game plan. We had to be a bit more direct and certain situations but it definitely affected the way we played, yes."

Gotham will conclude play at Sports Illustrated Stadium next Sunday at 3 p.m. local time in the NWSL semifinals against the Kansas City Current. The Red Bulls, who missed the MLS Cup playoffs for a second consecutive season, will host another match the night before, this time a friendly against Club America during the men's international break.

The pitch was an understandable obstacle for both teams but Gotham's struggles did not end there. The reigning champions, who are favored to win the championship for the third time in four seasons after winning the Shield, were second-best against the lowest-seeded team in the postseason. They benefitted from a fourth minute own goal from Jordyn Bugg, forced by standout Jaedyn Shaw, but were unable to actually assert any sort of dominance as the game progressed.

An unfortunate own goal and Gotham take the early lead ‼️NWSL Playoffs presented by Google Pixel pic.twitter.com/4LwZdfgLpx

Gotham did not take a single shot on target over the course of the game, their six shots totaling just 0.17 expected goals. The Reign were not all that much better but momentum shifted their way in the second half, eventually racking up 11 shots and 0.54 expected goals. The visitors were stymied by Gotham defenders Tierna Davidson and Jess Carter, as well as 2024 goalkeeper of the year Ann-Katrin Berger.

"She literally does it on a consistent basis," Shaw said about Berger. "It's crazy the kind of saves that she makes and I feel like she makes a worldly save at least once a game and I mean I think it's hard enough getting through a back line but to get through Ann is a whole other task and I think we're all really grateful to have her back there. I know I am as an attacker and I think we all just have full trust in her ability and she's just such an integral part of our team and the way that we like to play as well. Even from the goal, she's such a big piece of the way that we play and our style."

AKB goes aerial to deny Mia Fishel a goal ✈️ pic.twitter.com/4lqMm623On

Gotham's attack, though, had no such excuses. Midfielder Rose Lavelle exited the match at halftime as the coaching staff manages her minutes after dealing with a knock in recent weeks, her exit diluting their attack. Forward Sam Kerr, meanwhile, failed to register a single shot and took just 23 touches over the course of 90 minutes in an absent performance during an inconsistent return to the NWSL. The Australia international has scored just four goals in 18 games since joining Gotham in July, despite the fact that she has racked up 9.67 expected goals along the way.

Amoros credited the Reign for their ability to lock out Gotham's defense.

"I think they did a good job trying to stop certain situations," he said. "I think that was the key. They did really well on the press. They were first and second in a lot of the duels and they obviously play short passes to then go diagonal, which obviously then is something difficult to defend and something that is a lot more doable than probably over a style of play. It's just different and we had issues with those situations to defend. At the same time, we defended them. I think that's the key."

Shaw, who attempted to spearhead a lifeless Gotham attack, described a disjointed performance that the team will hope not to replicate the following week.

"I think we just need to be cleaner on the ball," Shaw said. "Obviously, the surface doesn't really help but  just in general, I think we can be more comfortable on the ball, facing forward and just be clinical in our passes, which I think will help us get to the final third a little bit more with more quality chances on goal."

#1151. How USMNT's Neil Pierre turned overseas loan into breakout season with Philadelphia Union

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

CHESTER, Pa. - Walking into Philadelphia Union training, there's one player who immediately sticks out due to towering over the rest of the team at center back: Neil Pierre. While a soft-spoken person in life, when you're 6-foot-7 on a soccer field, it's hard to miss him—even down to Chris Richards not believing it until he saw the Union defender in the United States Men's National Team camp. But height may also be the least interesting thing about Pierre's journey as he, like the Union, has taken MLS by storm since he returned from a loan spell in Denmark with Lyngby, where he helped the club gain promotion back to the Danish Superliga while getting a taste of what first-team soccer is like.

For an 19-year-old, just going to a new country is enough of an adjustment, and doing so while needing to break into a squad with ambition is quite a task, and Pierre did it while also learning a new position. Because of the club setup, Pierre actually played right back, and explaining the setup to CBS Sports, one of his co-managers, Andreas Bjelland, wanted to find out how he could get the talented young defender into the squad.

"He had the power, he had the drive, but he still needed the game smartness and the calmness of playing more senior minutes," Bjelland said. "And then he could get some extra minutes playing right back because we also had some really good center backs at that point playing really well. So it was a little bit of a mix of also getting him into play more and more."

This is a credit not only to Pierre's talent but also to his drive and versatility, as the Union man turned this into an excellent breakout where he scored four goals in 10 appearances while winning promotion and building confidence that he could do it as a soccer player along the way. Both the Union Academy and Pierre's own family helped set him up for success in a year that has become an absolute whirlwind. Following his success at Lyngby, alongside the Union falling to the bottom of the league, it was easy to question why Pierre wasn't with the team to start the season, but his time in Denmark was also formative. While it's easy to say that he should've been in Philadelphia from the start in hindsight, it was an important step for the Pierre that we see before us today.

"In the beginning, it was definitely a little nerve-wracking and definitely nervous," Pierre said, reflecting during Philadelphia Union training. "I think I can give all credit to them; they've kind of taken me in as like a part of the family immediately, so I felt like there was no stress there, and then that translated to on the pitch and they gave me the confidence to play how I was supposed to play. And then also off the field, I think, because we would go to team outings all the time and get dinner together, so it was like a family on and off the field."

Fast forward, and not only has Pierre been part of pulling the Union out of the bottom of the Eastern Conference, but he's also earned his first USMNT call-up and cap, and that was quickly followed by a return call for Concacaf Nations League play, where the USMNT will face Haiti twice during this international window, but if not for his family, soccer may not have happened. When Pierre was younger, basketball was the first sport that he connected with, but he credits his brother Nelson Pierre (who is currently on loan from the Vancouver Whitecaps to the HFX Wanderers of the Canadian Premier League) and his father for why he is where he is now.

"If it wasn't for them, I would be playing basketball right now. 100%," Pierre said. "But I think through them it was like I saw the love they had for the sport, and like how much passion they had, so I was like obviously I wanted to follow in my dad and brother's footsteps and be able to have that passion for something. So then I followed them into soccer and it's been since ever since it's been like this."

Considering his play for the Union this season, plenty are happy that Pierre made the decision to stick with soccer, but while his frame and closing speed do come with advantages, they also comes with things that he has to watch out for on the field, especially when defending against smaller players. Not only are they at times more agile than Pierre, but challenges that he makes can look worse too, and these are things that gaining more in-game experience has helped him prepare for, dealing with them and excelling.

He also has the benefit of playing not only for a coach that he knows from the Union youth ranks, but also for one who was a defender during his own professional career. In fact, Pierre has always had a defensive-minded head coach, even with the USMNT in Mauricio Pochettino, and that's something else that has been a benefit while he's getting his feet in the game.

"Obviously, being young, playing with older players [my coaches have] pulled me aside, either showing me film or what they feel like they've seen, and it's obviously different hearing it from a coach that's played in your position and done it at the highest level," Pierre said. "Same with the national team with Poch, I think hearing stuff like that, it's like these guys have done it at a pro level for a long time, so they know what they're talking about."

Add that to his natural skills, and you get a young defender that the Union can anchor the squad around. Before even getting into his goals, his closing speed and positioning are able to anchor a defense that has allowed the third-fewest goals in MLS since the World Cup, with only 21. They may not have risen to first in the Eastern Conference, but when the squad only had seven points prior to the World Cup and has picked up 40 after it so far, the impact that Pierre and the rest of the squad have had to push their way into the playoffs has been quite remarkable. You can also see why Lyngby wanted to keep him for their season in the Danish top flight, but when the Union had a chance at a starting spot, it was hard to allow Pierre to go back on loan when he could help the first team.

"We can be super aggressive because Neil is comfortable in one-on-one situations. If it's a direct ball, he wins; he eats all of these. If it's open space that he has to defend, physically, he can deal with that, and he's also a good defender," Philly's interim coach, Ryan Richter, said about how Pierre's play impacts his squad. "The way he puts out so many fires allows us to be aggressive higher up the field, because we know when they play the ball long that we have someone who cleans this up almost every time."

Defenders usually peak later than attackers in soccer, so it's impressive that Pierre is catching on so quickly, but given his path of getting into first-team soccer and also being with the coach who he came up through the academy with, it's a good spot for Pierre to succeed and grow before his next step likely takes him back to Europe.

"I think as a person, he's much more mature and much more focused than I would say at the point he was at a year ago, when I was coaching him with the second team. I'm really proud of him, the way that he's been able to put focus on the day-to-day and the game-to-game," Richter said. "Because I think of a lot of things, positive and negative, that happened to him this year. Having a great experience in Denmark, but it didn't start out perfect, and he earned his way in. When he came back here, he earned the starting spot. A couple months later called for the national team for his first caps to the national team. Comes back and is able to right away again put his full attention back in with the team and play a couple of good games after that. Um, so overall, his maturity in dealing with the things that are going on around him, I think, has been really impressive."

Pierre credits his family and the team for helping him stay grounded through what has been an absolute whirlwind year. Next up is a trip to USMNT camp before helping anchor the defense for the club as they face the New England Revolution in the first round of the MLS Cup playoffs. Plenty for a young player to juggle, but after the year Pierre has had, this will feel more normal than what he has already accomplished.

#1149. Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

What do football fans actually want from their club owners? The model for most has been Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and friends at Manchester City, owners whose hands are put frequently into pockets of unlimited depth, have made vast improvements to every aspect of the club and its community and are rarely ever seen, let alone heard from.

That view may have to evolve after certain verdicts about certain charges, but few envious glances from around the country have been cast towards the owners of Manchester’s other major club.

Manchester United’s accounts for last season suggest that ownership could be changing in the next three years, with a route to Sir Jim Ratcliffe assuming full control by 2029. But who would actually be the better custodians for United?

I’m good. It’s one of them – when you’ve had a result like we have, maybe a spell like we have, it definitely makes you hungry to push on and improve things. That’s what we have done this week.

We know it’s not been good enough. It’s obvious to say that. But it’s something we can flip and we are the ones who can control that. That’s the beauty of it for me. We are in control of it and know there’s something we can do about it.

I don’t need any assurances [from the board]. I totally understand what’s needed here. I’m just focused on winning games.

If there’s anything I take about beyond these four walls it’s how the supporters are thinking. That’s all that matters to me. I’m not interested [in external noise in the media etc], my only focus is on making us better.

[Do you think the players are behind you?] One hundred per cent, for sure.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

#1148. UEFA Women's Champions League: Matchday 4 storylines as USWNT stars in action, Arsenal face Barcelona

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Time is ticking away in the 2026-27 UEFA Women's Champions League. Three matchdays have been played, and now just three remain in the league phase. The landscape has shifted from which clubs look good to the ones who can still afford to build slowly in the 18-team table.

Matchday 4 will scatter games from Tuesday to Thursday, with Chelsea away to face BK Hacken to kick off the action, and current title holders FC Barcelona and Arsenal close out the narrowing league phase. OL Lyonnes and Juventus will clash to determine who remains among the top contenders and who scrambles for points with just a few opportunities left.

There's no more time for slow starts, and every result carries more weight than the last, which means it's time for teams who have yet to notch any wins, like UWCL hopefuls Real Madrid and Manchester City.

Fans can watch all the action across CBS Sports platforms. Paramount+ will livestream matches all season, while select fixtures will also air on CBS Sports Golazo Network and CBS Sports Network. With Matchday 4 split across three days, here are three things we're keeping an eye on:

Fans will have to wait till later in the week for a heavyweight battle between Barcelona and Arsenal on Thursday. A win by either side could change the league phase table and set the tone for the final two rounds.

Barcelona have scored 19 goals over their opening three matches and sit top of the table with nine points, and every fixture that passes gives us new reasons to never doubt them. They're coming off a massive win against HB Koge where they demolished the Danish side 8-0, and Claudia Pina had a standout performance with two goals and two assists.

TWO GOALS AND AN ASSIST FOR CLÀUDIA PINA 🤩🔥The Spaniard grabs her second of the night as Barcelona's attacking masterclass continues 🎓Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/2PzEf1FbRv

The Catalonians are reigning title holders and have shown no signs of slowing down in the tournament, even with the departures of familiar faces in Alexia Putellas and Salma Paralluelo. Now they'll face Arsenal, the squad that handed them a runners-up finish just two seasons ago.

Despite some questionable form and tactics to start the tournament, Arsenal are now third on the league phase table with seven points. It hardly sounds like a bad place to be, but how they got there is what raises concerns. A stoppage-time penalty on opening day, followed by a draw where they let a two-goal lead slip, did little to settle any doubts about how the Gunners were playing.

But a more convincing win over Benfica propelled the club into good standing on the league phase table, and now they face their biggest challenge of the tournament. Manager Renee Slegers is just two seasons removed from rallying the side against a lethal Barcelona, and Alessa Russo looks almost unstoppable in front of goal at the moment. The real battle will be in the midfield, and whether or not Arsenal can stop Barcelona from moving the ball.

If they find a way to disrupt that rhythm and create some problems, then maybe they can produce a clean chance on goal; otherwise, Barcelona will have their way like they have all tournament long.

It might be hard to believe, but even after three matchdays, there are still teams with expectations who have not picked up wins.

Manchester City will face Inter Milan on Tuesday after three consecutive draws in the tournament. A frustrating theme follows the Women's Super League champions, who just can't seem to replicate their domestic success in top European competition. Bunny Shaw has scored two goals, one against Real Madrid and a penalty conversion against PSG, and the roster will expect more when Manchester City go up against the debutant Inter.

Real Madrid are in a similar position. After drawing all three of their league phase games to date, they now face a tricky Paris FC side at home. Linda Caicedo finally has more attackers alongside her in Felicia Schroder and Lineth Beerensteyn, who seems healthy and ready to score. The club have yet to establish themselves as a bona fide contender, and they'll need to get wins if they want to prove that they belong in VIP instead of outside in line waiting to get into the club.

Paris FC could be motivated by the absence of captain Clara Mateo, who will be out serving a red card suspension, and Evelyne Viens is always a factor on the pitch. A win by the Parisians could easily shake up the league phase table and leapfrog Real Madrid.

Barcelona and Arsenal aren't the only clubs in good standing heading into Matchday 4. OL Lyonnes are second on the league phase table with seven points after two blowout wins against Servette and Inter Milan, and a scoreless draw against Chelsea.

The French giants will travel to Italy and face Juventus, a side that seems to be waking up at the right time of the tournament. OL have plenty of attacking talent with Melchie Dumornay and Marie-Antoinette Katoto, and Katoto leads the Golden Boot race with five goals scored over three matchdays. Lily Yohannes, 19, protects the midfield, and the U.S. women's national team player has already made her mark with a long-range chip shot.

LILY YOHANNES, THAT IS SPECIAL! 🇺🇸🔥The 19-year-old American with a stunning strike ✨Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/OlHOa7BbdS

Juventus have quietly racked up enough points in the league phase to keep them in good standing in fifth place with six points and have shown they're no pushovers. They settled for a 3-3 draw against OL Lyonnes last season, and their wins this year against Austria Wien and Hacken have given them some margin for errors should any arise against any tournament favorites. A win by either side on Wednesday and they'll separate in the standings.

Chelsea FC are using defense to get through the opening stages of the Champions League. In fourth place with seven points over three games, the Blues have yet to concede a goal in the league phase. They'll be tested against Hacken in Sweden, a side desperate for points. But Alyssa Thompson's efforts on the wing could help ease some things, and Wieke Kaptein has been the roster's MVP in the first half of the league phase.

In a battle of what are we even doing here? Bayern Munich will face Paris Saint-Germain in France in a match that could truly decide which of them even stays in the conversation for top four or knockout playoffs. Both teams are on five points, and are better at settling for draws than winning in the competition, but either way, neither can afford a loss when they meet on Tuesday.
